extracted.intended_audience: patent lawyers, judges, and law students
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on legal tests and evidentiary rules for determining infringement of patents (machines, manufactures, and processes), including the doctrines of substantial identity and mechanical equivalents. Focuses on how differences of form, modes of operation, and evidence of process affect infringement findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement involves substantial identity
rubrics_metrics.description: An infringement involves substantial identity, whether that identity is described by the terms, "same principle," "same modus operandi," or any other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is a copy of the thing described in the specification of the patentee, either without variation, or with only such variations as are consistent with its being in substance the same thing. What will amount to such a substantial identity cannot be stated in general terms; look to individual cases for illustrations and applications of the general doctrine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of a machine = peculiar structure or constituent parts
rubrics_metrics.description: The true legal meaning of the principle of a machine, with reference to the patent, is the peculiar structure or constituent parts of such machine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Skilful witnesses may be asked whether the principles of two machines are the same or different. The principles may be the same even though form or proportions differ (same power employed in same way), or different despite external similarity. Care must be taken to distinguish the legal sense of 'principle' from a generic meaning (e.g., 'motion').

rubrics_metrics.name: Machine infringement test — performs same service/effect in same way
rubrics_metrics.description: A machine will be infringed by a machine which incorporates in its structure and operation the substance of the invention; that is, by an arrangement of mechanism, which performs the same service, or produces the same effect in the same way, or substantially in the same way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare mode of operation and the substance of the claimed invention (Wyeth v. Stone example). Minor differences (e.g., double vs single series of cutters) may be immaterial if the substance and mode are substantially the same.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mere colorable alterations insufficient to avoid infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not in the power of any other person, simply by varying in form or in immaterial circumstances, the nature or subject-matter of that discovery, to obtain either a patent for it himself, or to use it without the leave of the patentee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Must examine whether, in reality, in substance, and in effect, the defendant has availed himself of the plaintiff's invention. Slight or colorable variations designed to evade the patent can be disregarded (Walton v. Potter; Davis v. Palmer).

rubrics_metrics.name: Material alteration v. mere difference of form
rubrics_metrics.description: The material question is not whether the same elements of motion, or the same component parts are used, but whether the given effect is produced substantially by the same mode of operation, and the same combination of powers, in both machines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mere colorable differences or slight improvements cannot shake the right of the original inventor. Examples: additions of minute functions (minutes/seconds hands) do not permit patenting the whole if using same combinations and mode; jury decides factual questions of materiality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanical equivalents doctrine — identity of purpose, not form
rubrics_metrics.description: The doctrine depends upon the truth that the identity of purpose, and not of form or name, is the true criterion in judging of the similarity or dissimilarity of two pieces of mechanism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether one thing is a mechanical equivalent for another is a question of fact for the jury, based on expert testimony or inspection. Consider whether the defendant's contrivance is used for the same purpose, performs the same duties, or is applicable to the same object. Names and forms are of comparatively little importance; look to substance, not form (Morgan v. Seaward; Alderson instruction).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanical equivalents depend on circumstances; advantages do not absolve infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: Two things may be mechanical equivalents for each other under some circumstances, which would not be so under different circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a defendant's change constitutes a mechanical equivalent and also accomplishes some other advantage beyond the effect accomplished by the patentee, it will still be an infringement as respects what is covered by the patent, although the further advantage may be patentable as an improvement. Examples include variations in chain-link construction or use of different parts serving different duties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvement patents limited to the improvement; cannot claim prior inventions
rubrics_metrics.description: If another person invents an improvement on such a machine, he can entitle himself to a patent for such improvement only, and does not thereby acquire a right to patent and use the original machine; and if he does procure a patent for the whole of such a machine with the improvement, and not for the improvement only, his patent is too broad, and therefore void.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An improver may obtain exclusivity for his improvement but cannot lawfully use the original inventor's discovery without license. The law awards exclusive property to each discovery but prevents one from invading the other's rights (examples: Read v. Perkins discussion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Manufacture-subject test — same plan applied to same purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the subject-matter of the patent is a manufacture, the same test of substantial identity is to be applied. The question will be, whether in reality and in substance the defendant has availed himself of the invention of the patentee, in order to make the fabric or article which he has made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Varying the form or process of application will not necessarily avoid infringement if the defendant has taken the same plan and applied it to the same purpose (Walton v. Potter India-rubber card example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Similarity of appearance/structure is presumptive evidence of same process (for process patents)
rubrics_metrics.description: Similarity in appearance and structure will not of itself always establish an infringement; because the patent, though it covers the manufactured article itself, may be for the process of the manufacture. ... The similarity of structure of two things is presumptive evidence of their being made in the same way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where sole evidence consists of similarity of articles, the inference that the same process was used must be drawn from the evidence. Similarity plus evidence of use of similar apparatus strengthens the presumption (Huddart v. Grimshaw; Hall v. Boot). But the rule is not absolute and depends on whether the article could be produced by other substantially different processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof on plaintiff; manufacture vs process distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: The burden of proof is always on the plaintiff to show that his process has been infringed; and in the absence of direct evidence, the similarity of the effect produced will generally be sufficient to establish an infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the invention is a manufacture, it is immaterial by what process it is produced: making the same thing suffices. If the invention is a process, the inquiry is whether the article was made by the process covered by the patent; the identity of the manufactured article, together with other circumstances, is evidence from which the jury may infer use of the patentee's process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patents claiming application of a principle — focus on substantial identity of application
rubrics_metrics.description: Wherever the real subject covered by the patent is the application of a principle, in arts or manufactures, the question, on an infringement, will be as to the substantial identity of the principle, and of the application of the principle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Means, machinery, forms, or modifications of matter are material only so far as they affect the identity of the application of the principle. First form a clear idea of the object of the patent and what the specification properly points out as the patentee's claim (intro to §229–230).
